newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian scientists see genetically enhanced wines.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian scientists see genetically enhanced wines.

text.p: A team of Australian researchers has raised hopes for the production of superior grapes after successful tests to genetically modify vines.
The team in this South Australian city said on Tuesday it had also produced stay-white potatoes which could cut costs and chemical use by the producers of chips and crisps.
Team leader Nigel Scott said the new vines could transform the country's wine and dried fruit industries by boosting productivity and quality.
"Using this technology, we can create grapevines with enhanced flavour, improved colour development and increased disease resistance," Scott told Reuters.

Scott said the team, funded by the government's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), had produced about 20 grape vines from single cells in a test tube environment, each vine containing a new introduced gene.

He said the three-strong team had in 1991 isolated vine genes which were responsible for differing characters, such as colour and sugar accumulation, but had been searching since for a system to return genes in a modified form into grape vines.
"That is what we have now," Scott said.
The breakthrough had come in the successful use in grape vines of a special bacterium, widely employed as a "taxi" to transport a novel gene into plant DNA (dioxyribonucleic acid).
"It is a tool which is used for most transformations of plants but for grape vines it has been more difficult," he said.
"It is the last piece of the jigsaw puzzle we need."
Scott acknowledged similar developments in genetically-transformed vines from other molecular geneticists in France, Israel and the United States.

He said the Adelaide team had grown only test plants to date, with the production of grapes from modified vines at least two years away. Given approval from regulatory authorities, it expected to be able to begin field tests in 1998, he said.

Scott said the research would move onto colouring genes in other wine grape vines, including the premium chardonnay and cabernet varieties, which could reduce the need for sulphur dioxide in white wines and enhance the colour of red varieties.

It would also try to adapt the process to isolate genes which prevent the most damaging vineyard diseases -- downy mildew, powdery mildew and botrytis -- and to genes involved in the accumulation of sugar in the grape. The researchers are partly funded by the Australian wine industry.

Scott said the new vines had the potential to reap hundreds of millions of dollars in benefits for the A$1.5 billion (US$1.2 billion) annual wine and dried fruit industries, adding it could take six years before all processes could be reliably tested.
The new vines have been welcomed by Australia's thriving wine industry, which is enjoying steadily increasing exports on a reputation for clean, fruity and good-value wines.

Announcing the development, leading Australian winemaker Brian Croser said: "The opportunity to introduce disease resistance and other valuable characteristics without changing the essential quality of varieties offers Australia its biggest potential gains in the winery and the vineyard".
On the back of the same research, the CSIRO team also expects soon to sign with a major investor to develop a gene which stops peeled and sliced potatoes turning brown.
Scott said the development -- already successfully tested -- would be a major boost for the chips and crisps industries, which currently uses heat and sulphur dioxide to stop browning.
"The results were really quite dramatic: when you cut the potatoes open and leave them on the kitchen bench or on the laboratory bench in this case, they do not go brown," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 612-9373-1800
